questions.prompt: Which of the following are mentioned in 'The Shift from School to College'? Select all that apply.
options: Nobody chases missing work. Responsibility is yours
You have more unstructured time and must manage it yourself
Problems often appear weeks or months after the original mistake
Independence is expected and developed through practice
questions.explanation: All of these are mentioned in the section on The Shift from School to College.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the deck's honest contrast between school and college?
options: 'At college, your day is filled in for you.'
'At college, a bad week shows up next week.'
'At college, no one chases — the work is yours, or it doesn't get done.'
'At college, teachers check your reading every morning.'
questions.explanation: 'No one chases. The work is yours — or it doesn't get done.'

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: students who do better don't work harder — they just ____ in advance.
questions.template: Students who do better don't work harder — they just ____ in advance.
options: decide
recover
submit
complain
questions.explanation: They just decide in advance what their free periods are for.

questions.prompt: Which of these does the deck suggest for Seek Opportunity? Select all that apply.
options: Enter a short film or digital media competition
Build a public portfolio on Behance or Vimeo
Research BA degrees at University Centre Hastings or Higher Apprenticeship routes
Wait until your teacher tells you to start a portfolio
questions.explanation: All three are concrete examples of Seek Opportunity behaviours in the deck.

questions.prompt: How does the deck say most students feel in their first weeks at college?
options: Settled and confident
Bored because it is easier than school
Out of depth — and that's a sign they've moved up, not that they're in the wrong place
Certain they chose the wrong course
questions.explanation: Most students feel out of depth in their first weeks — not some, most. It's a sign you've moved up, not that you're in the wrong place.

questions.prompt: On attendance, the deck deliberately uses…
options: Specific percentage thresholds and warnings
A plain case about what you actually lose when you're not in the room
A list of formal consequences
Threats of course removal
questions.explanation: The deck deliberately avoids percentage thresholds. The case is made in terms of what you actually lose.

questions.prompt: Which of these are part of the deck's plain case for attendance? Select all that apply.
options: The bit that isn't on the slides — off-script teaching, worked examples
Spaced learning that actually sticks
The relationships that catch you when you slip
Being seen by the people writing your reference
questions.explanation: All four are the plain-case arguments the deck uses.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are mentioned in 'The "Long Fuse" Principle'? Select all that apply.
options: Missing brief reviews, lessons or coursework now creates gaps later
Catching up becomes harder when new work is arriving at the same time
Planning free periods in advance helps prevent this
questions.explanation: All of these are mentioned in the section on The "Long Fuse" Principle.
